Nestlings of the Eurasian tree sparrow (Passer montanus) emerge from calcareous eggs after a well-defined incubation period. Eggs maintained at a constant temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C] hatch after approximately 13 days [ab = approximately 13 days], a developmental duration consistent with that of other small-bodied passerines in the family Passeridae. At the moment of hatching, these altricial chicks weigh approximately 2.2 grams [Wwb = approximately 2.2 grams], a mass that reflects the considerable energetic investment in yolk reserves during embryogenesis. This relatively low neonatal mass places the tree sparrow among the smaller-bodied members of its genus, with a birth weight comparable to that of the house sparrow (Passer domesticus). The initial fragility of the newly hatched chick is offset by the onset of intensive biparental care, during which both parents contribute to brooding and provisioning, ensuring the nestling's rapid growth trajectory during the critical early days of life. Studies in both captive and wild populations confirm these values, underscoring the species’ altricial developmental strategy.

During the nestling phase, which unfolds under an average body temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], chicks achieve several key developmental milestones. The time since birth at fledging is approximately 14 days [tx = approximately 14 days], a relatively brief period that allows young birds to leave the nest cavity and begin exploring their immediate surroundings at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This early fledging age, measured from hatching, is characteristic of many secondary cavity-nesting species that rely on enclosed nests for protection against predators and adverse weather. Once out of the nest, fledglings remain dependent on parental provisioning for an additional one to two weeks, gradually developing the foraging skills necessary for independent survival. The rapid departure from the nest is thought to be an adaptive response to the high risk of nest predation in open agricultural landscapes, where these sparrows are commonly found foraging in mixed-species flocks. This developmental pace is consistent with the high reproductive output observed in this species.

Sexual maturation in Passer montanus occurs after a distinct post-fledging interval. Under the thermal conditions typical of the active metabolic period in this species, 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], puberty is attained at 42 days after hatching [tp = 42 days after hatching]. This relatively early onset of gonadal maturity allows young birds to potentially breed in their first calendar year, a life-history strategy common among small temperate-zone passerines that face intense seasonal constraints on breeding opportunities. Field observations suggest that the onset of reproductive activity is closely tied to photoperiod and food availability, and individuals that reach this developmental stage later in the season may delay breeding until the following spring. The full expression of sexually dimorphic plumage characteristics, including the characteristic chestnut crown and black bib, typically coincides with the completion of the first prebasic molt. These features signal readiness for the reproductive phase.

First reproduction in Eurasian tree sparrows typically occurs at approximately 319 days after hatching [tR = approximately 319 days after hatching], a value measured under ambient conditions at 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This timing reflects a strategy whereby young birds delay their first breeding attempt until the spring following their birth year, likely to maximize the probability of successful nesting. Females typically produce clutches of 5 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 5 eggs per clutch], and they may complete one or two nesting attempts per year, yielding a maximum reproductive rate of approximately 2.5 clutches yearly [F_R_i = approximately 2.5 clutches yearly]. The relatively high fecundity of this species, combined with its early sexual maturity, contributes to its success as a colonist of urban and agricultural habitats across its extensive Palearctic range. Such reproductive flexibility allows population persistence under variable conditions.

Longevity records for the Eurasian tree sparrow indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 13.1 years [am = approximately 13.1 years] for individuals maintained under controlled conditions at 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This exceptional longevity for a bird of its body size is noteworthy, as most small passerines rarely survive beyond five years in the wild. The ultimate adult mass, an asymptotic weight reached by fully grown individuals, is approximately 25 grams [Wwi = approximately 25 grams], a value that is slightly lower than the typical adult mass due to continued skeletal and muscular development in older birds. Mortality in wild populations is highest during the first winter, with predation and food scarcity being the primary agents of death; only a small fraction of individuals survive to reach the maximum lifespan reported here. Senescence in this species is characterized by a gradual decline in reproductive output and immune function rather than a catastrophic physiological collapse. These demographic patterns are consistent with a slow life-history strategy among small passerines.
